analysis.one_liner: Bans spanking, paddling, and other physical punishment of students in schools that get federal money.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate education committee in May 2023, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would ban corporal punishment — deliberate acts that cause physical pain for discipline, including striking, spanking, paddling, painful restraints, and the use of chemical sprays or stun guns — in every school that receives federal money. Students or parents could sue a school that paddles them; the Education Department could withhold federal funds or issue cease-and-desist orders; and schools would have to report any use of force to parents, state officials, and police within 24 hours. It also creates grants to help schools switch to positive behavioral supports instead of physical punishment and suspensions.
analysis.who_benefits: Students in the roughly 17 states that still allow paddling and other physical discipline — disproportionately students with disabilities and students of color — would gain a federal right not to be hit at school, plus a way to sue and federal enforcement if schools ignore it. Parents would learn within 24 hours if their child was struck. Schools would get grant money to train staff in alternatives to physical discipline.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students in states that allow paddling

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it illegal for any school personnel, school-assigned law enforcement officer, or security guard at a federally funded school to deliberately inflict physical pain on a student for discipline, including striking, paddling, painful positioning, and chemical sprays or stun guns [S3].

A student or parent who is subjected to corporal punishment can sue the school for damages and injunctive relief, and the Education Department must investigate complaints, potentially withholding federal funds or issuing cease-and-desist orders against schools that fail to comply [S2][S3].

Schools must report any use of physical force on a student to parents, the state education agency, and law enforcement within 24 hours, and for students with disabilities, also to the state protection and advocacy system [S3].

The bill authorizes three-year grants to states, passed through to school districts, to train staff in positive behavioral interventions, restorative justice, and trauma-informed care as alternatives to paddling and suspensions [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: School districts, mainly in states that still permit corporal punishment, would bear the cost of changing discipline practices, training staff, and filing state school-climate reports. Taxpayers fund the new grant program, which has no specified dollar amount. Teachers, security staff, and police officers assigned to schools would lose the ability to use physical discipline, though the bill preserves sworn officers' lawful duties outside the ban.

drawbacks.text: The enforcement tool is withholding federal education funds, and critics of this approach argue that cutting school money ends up hurting the students the law is meant to protect; the bill softens this by requiring reimbursement of withheld funds if a school cures the violation within a year [S3].
The private right of action lets families sue schools for damages and attorney's fees, which could expose school districts to litigation costs over individual discipline incidents [S3].

The bill conditions all federal education money on discipline rules, which some view as federal overreach into decisions that states and local school boards have historically made; states with their own bans or no corporal punishment are barely affected [S3].
The grant program and reporting requirements are authorized without a funding limit, creating an open-ended federal expense if enacted [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete and narrow: it stops schools from paddling or spraying children, a practice a minority of states still permit and that falls disproportionately on students with disabilities. The main costs fall on the school districts still using the practice and on taxpayers for the training grants, and the bill's own design limits the harshest cost (withheld funds are reimbursed if the violation is fixed within a year). A fair reading is that the benefits are real but geographically limited, while the paperwork and reporting obligations apply nationwide.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Murphy introduced the bill in May 2023 and it was sent straight to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Murphy introduced the bill on May 30, 2023 with five original cosponsors, including Senators Brown, Casey, Durbin, Sanders, and Van Hollen [S1][S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; that referral was the last action the bill ever received [S5].
The bill attracted eight total cosponsors — seven of the Senate's 48 Democrats and one of its four independents — and no Republican support [S4].
With no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote ever scheduled over the remaining 19 months of the Congress, the bill expired with no vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained directly from the bill dying, but schools in the states that still allow corporal punishment kept their existing practices, and local districts avoided the compliance, reporting, and litigation exposure the bill would have imposed. Students who are paddled or sprayed at school remain without a federal remedy.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Schools that paddle students kept their practice

for.name: Sen. Chris Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill in the 19 months after referral.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party split is recorded; the bill's eight cosponsors were all Democrats or independents and no Republican signed on [S4].

industries.industry: School districts in states that permit corporal punishment
industries.note: These districts would lose the option of paddling students and would face lawsuits, 24-hour reporting duties, and possible loss of federal funds. Their interest in keeping the practice runs against the students being hit.

industries.industry: Private schools not receiving federal support
industries.note: The bill expressly leaves private schools and home schools untouched unless they accept federal funds or serve federally supported students, preserving their freedom to use physical discipline even as public schools are barred from it.

industries.industry: Federal taxpayers and the Education Department
industries.note: The department gains new enforcement duties and taxpayers fund an open-ended grant program for school climate training, in exchange for enforcing a student safety rule.
